response.text:
Sifted out of the duke and duchess’s luxurious pranks, Sancho resigns his brief, hungry, and harried governorship of Barataria and stumbles back to his master with a new distrust of the “remedies” that make him the cow of everyone’s wedding. Don Quixote, by turns exalted and despondent, passes through new pageantries and rigged enchantments—Altisidora’s staged death and resurrection at his expense, duennas with pins and smacks for Sancho, and the sardonic civility of great hosts who treat knight-errantry as a court comedy. In Barcelona the pair glimpse the sea for the first time, are carried in triumph to Don Antonio Moreno’s house, and are beguiled by a “talking head” that confidently answers questions until its clever ventilation tube is revealed. Meanwhile Don Quixote’s chivalric fantasy collides with contemporary politics when they visit the galleys and help free the fair Morisca Ana Félix and her disguised lover Don Gregorio, even as her father Ricote’s piety and prudence cast a sober light on Spain’s expulsions.

On the beach at Barcelona, fate turns in earnest: the Knight of the White Moon (really the bachelor Samson Carrasco, now in a second disguise) unhorses Don Quixote and exacts the vow that he retire home for a year. The defeat sours his buoyancy, and even Sancho’s clowning cannot sweeten it, though he busies himself with halter and headstall to counterfeit the self-scourgings Merlin required for Dulcinea’s disenchantment. Harried by a grunting drove of pigs and goaded by omens that Sancho cheerfully dismisses, they trudge homeward, stopping long enough at a Seville printing-house for Don Quixote to denounce the spurious continuation of his story and to extract a notarial declaration from Don Álvaro Tarfe that the “other” Don Quixote is a sham. Through such scenes the book’s mirrors multiply—jokes inside pranks, performances confronting a crowd—until the sport and the satire begin to weigh upon the players.

Back in La Mancha, his niece and housekeeper weeping, Don Quixote first surveys a final escape: a pastoral metamorphosis into the shepherd Quixotiz, with Carrascon (Samson), Curambro (the curate), and Pancino (Sancho) crooning among the beech trees. But the body that could weather a thousand comic batterings yields to a real fever, and the mind that trafficked in enchantments regains its plain name, Alonso Quixano the Good. He repudiates the “profane stories” that misled him, makes a careful will—pardoning Sancho’s muddled accounts and enjoining his niece to avoid husbands who read books of chivalry—and begs his friends to warn off any future impostor who would drag him, falsely, back from the grave. Sancho pleads for one more sally and blames the girths for the defeat, but his master, calm and devout, will not be laughed back into life.

Cide Hamete Benengeli, the Moorish chronicler whose pen claims to match Don Quixote’s sword, closes the ledger with a gentle flourish: the Manchegan knight, whether mad or cured, inspired real love in those who knew him and now rests honorably as one who died wisely after living foolishly. The friends carve their epitaphs, the villagers return to their bread and wine, and the author, half-smiling, shelves his own pen with a brass wire, warning meddling continuators—like the Tordesillas usurper he has already skewered—to leave these weary bones in peace. Thus the illusion gives way to reckoning, the game to gravity: a life made of words ends in a plain confession, and the fame that chased Dulcinea’s shadow learns, at last, how to be still.
